title: I published my first iOS game using Claude Code.
author: rashidckk
selftext:
I've always wanted to develop my own mobile games. I know a bit of coding and have developed a few apps before, but I have absolutely zero skills in art or design.

When people suddenly started vibe coding games with Opus 5.5, I decided it was finally time for me to jump on the bandwagon.

Everyone seemed to be using Claude Code and Opus 5.5, so I went that route too. I subscribed to Claude Pro, installed Xcode on my Mac for iOS development, and renewed my Apple Developer account, which had been inactive for a while.

The first challenge was coming up with a game idea.

I'm not particularly creative when it comes to game ideas, so I had absolutely nothing in mind.

I'm a regular X user, and my feed was already full of people sharing the cool things they were building with Opus 5.5. While scrolling through it, I came across a pixel art image that really caught my attention. I liked it so much that I took a screenshot.

I uploaded the image to Claude (I use the desktop version) and asked it to suggest some game ideas that would work well with that art style.

It came up with several ideas. I picked one I liked and asked Claude Code to build the game.

I used Opus 5.5 with medium effort and specifically asked it to build a native iOS game.

I barely had to touch Xcode. Claude Code created the project, wrote the code, and even ran the game in the iOS simulator.

At one point, it asked me to provide background music. I generated the soundtrack using Google's Flow Music. I also added sound effects, which I created using ElevenLabs.

I didn't use sub-agents or any complicated multi-agent workflows. I simply worked directly with Claude Code, going back and forth with prompts, testing the game, and asking it to make improvements.

Once the game was ready, I asked Claude Code to prepare all the assets required for App Store submission. It even captured screenshots and screen recordings directly from the simulator.

I wanted to get everything right the first time and avoid an App Store rejection. Claude Code also guided me through the submission process and provided instructions for publishing.

After submitting the game, it took around 10 days for it to go live on the App Store. And It passed the review without a single rejection!

Btw, The game is called Pip's Way Home.

It's a calm, cozy puzzle game where you tap path tiles to rotate them and connect a glowing path from a campfire to Pip's cottage door. As you solve each puzzle, the little isle lights up.

I'd love to hear your feedback!

Get the game from [here](https://apps.apple.com/app/id6826500925).
